title: Manakish lahm bi ajeen
subtitle: Lebanese flatbread with spiced lamb and tomato
excerpt: Lahm bi ajeen (meat with dough) are small Lebanese flatbreads topped with a finely ground spiced lamb and tomato paste pressed into the surface before baking. They emerge from the oven crisp-edged, with a thin, cooked-through meat topping that is distinctly different from a pizza.
sourceNotes: Anissa Helou, Lebanese Cuisine (1994). Lahm bi ajeen described as one of the two principal manakish toppings, available at every Lebanese bakery. Claudia Roden, A Book of Middle Eastern Food (1968). Notes on the method and topping consistency.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze baked flatbreads before rolling. Reheat in a hot oven for three minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can rise overnight in the fridge. The lamb topping can be made a day ahead and refrigerated.
recipe.temperatureNote: Fan 220 degrees / gas 9. Preheat for at least 20 minutes.

content.text: Lahm bi ajeen are Lebanese flatbreads with a thin layer of very finely processed lamb and tomato paste pressed directly into the dough before baking. The lamb is almost pureed rather than minced, which means it cooks flat and evenly in the brief time the bread takes to bake. Eaten rolled up or flat, hot or warm, they are one of the best Levantine breakfast dishes.

Mix {{yeast-dried}} and {{caster-sugar}} into 185 ml of warm water. Leave five minutes until foamy. Combine {{strong-bread-flour}} and {{sea-salt-fine}} in a bowl. Add the yeast mixture and {{olive-oil}}, mix to a rough dough, and knead for eight minutes until smooth. Cover and prove for one hour.

Put {{onion}} and {{tomato}} in a food processor. Pulse until very finely chopped. Add {{lamb-mince}}, {{tomato-puree}}, {{allspice}}, {{cinnamon-ground}}, {{aleppo-pepper}}, and {{sea-salt-fine}}. Run for one minute until nearly smooth.
The mixture should be spreadable and slightly wet. If it is very wet, set it in a sieve for ten minutes to drain excess liquid.
Preheat the oven to 240 degrees. Divide the dough into six or eight pieces. Roll each piece very thin, about 2 mm, into rough circles or ovals. Lay on baking trays.
Spread a thin, even layer of the lamb mixture over each disc right to the edges. The layer should be thin enough that you can see the dough through it in places.

Bake for eight to ten minutes until the edges are golden, the base is crisp, and the lamb is cooked through. Squeeze {{lemon}} over and scatter {{parsley-flat}} if using. Eat immediately, rolled up or flat.

items.symptom: The lamb topping is still pink after ten minutes
items.cause: Layer too thick or oven not hot enough
items.fix: The lamb must be spread very thinly. A thick layer will not cook through in the short baking time. Cook for a further three minutes if needed.

items.symptom: The base is soft rather than crispy
items.cause: Dough too thick or oven not preheated long enough
items.fix: Roll the dough as thin as possible. Preheat the oven for at least 20 minutes with baking trays inside so the base starts cooking immediately.

items.symptom: The topping is watery and the bread goes soggy
items.fix: Drain the processed mixture through a sieve for ten minutes before using. The topping should be spreadable, not liquid.

items.symptom: The bread is too thick and bready
items.fix: Roll to 2 mm: much thinner than you think you need. Lahm bi ajeen should be cracker-thin at the edges.

content.text: Lahm bi ajeen (literally 'meat in dough' in Arabic) is one of the most ubiquitous street foods and bakery items across Lebanon, Syria, and the wider Levant. At a Lebanese furn, the flatbreads are baked continuously from early morning and sold stacked in papers to take away. They are eaten on the spot, rolled around a handful of fresh parsley and a squeeze of lemon. The dish is also common in Armenian and Syrian Christian communities, where it goes by the name lahmacun or lamajun. The Turkish lahmacun is closely related, though the Turkish version tends to be more heavily spiced and less tomato-forward.
